scenes.question: In HTL, what is the difference between data-sly-include and data-sly-resource?
scenes.heading: data-sly-include includes another HTL script in the same component context; data-sly-resource includes a JCR resource resolved by path, running its full Sling rendering pipeline
scenes.body: HTL includes: data-sly-include evaluates the referenced HTL/JSP script in the current Sling rendering context — same request, same resource, same resolver. data-sly-resource dispatches a new Sling include request for a JCR resource, which causes Sling to look up its sling:resourceType and render it through the full component rendering pipeline, including any associated Use-API objects and child scripts.

scenes.question: HTL-003 requires always specifying an explicit output context for URI expressions. Which context prevents open redirect and XSS attacks for href attribute values?
scenes.heading: context='uri' — validates the URI structure and strips dangerous javascript: and data: scheme prefixes
scenes.body: HTL-003 (Major): Without context='uri', an attacker can inject javascript:alert(1) as an href value. The default attribute context encodes HTML special characters but does NOT validate URI schemes. context='uri' applies URI scheme validation, blocking javascript:, data:, vbscript:, and other dangerous schemes. Safe schemes (http, https, relative paths, mailto, #anchors) pass through; unsafe ones are replaced with an empty string or '#', preventing protocol injection.

scenes.question: How does HTL's data-sly-list attribute iterate over a collection, and what implicit loop variables does it provide?
scenes.heading: data-sly-list.item='${model.items}' iterates the collection; provides itemList.index (0-based), itemList.count (1-based), itemList.first, itemList.last, itemList.odd, itemList.even
scenes.body: HTL data-sly-list: The syntax 'data-sly-list.item="${model.items}"' binds each element to 'item'. HTL automatically creates a companion variable 'itemList' (the loop variable name + 'List') with helper properties: .index (0-based), .count (1-based), .first (boolean), .last (boolean), .odd/.even (alternating booleans). These allow CSS class conditionals and element separators without Java logic.

scenes.question: HTL-005 (Severity: Minor) discourages inline CSS or JavaScript within HTL templates. What is the recommended approach for component styling and behavior?
scenes.heading: Use AEM Client Libraries (cq:ClientLibraryFolder) to deliver CSS and JS as versioned, cacheable assets linked via data-sly-call='${clientlib.all @ categories=...}'
scenes.body: HTL-005 (Minor): AEM Client Libraries (cq:ClientLibraryFolder) are the correct way to deliver CSS and JavaScript. They are versioned (via md5 fingerprinting in AEM CS), cached by the Dispatcher as long-lived static assets, combinable via categories to reduce HTTP requests, and tree-shaken in modern AEM setups. Inline CSS/JS in HTL is not cached, cannot be combined with other component styles, and pollutes the HTML response.

scenes.question: What is the purpose of HTL's context='numberLiteral' and context='styleToken' output contexts?
scenes.heading: numberLiteral allows only numeric characters (no quotes) for JS numeric values; styleToken allows only safe CSS identifiers (no special chars) for CSS values
scenes.body: HTL strict contexts: context='numberLiteral' restricts output to numeric characters only (digits, plus/minus signs, decimal point, exponent notation) — safe for embedding in JavaScript number literals without quotes. context='styleToken' restricts output to CSS-safe identifier characters (alphanumerics, hyphens, underscores) — safe for dynamic CSS class names or property values in style attributes. Both use allowlist filtering: any character not in the allowed set is stripped.
